newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans have lost faith in justice system - report.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans have lost faith in justice system - report.

text.p: Mexicans have lost faith in their justice system, which is a bloated, inefficient monster needing root and branch reform, an official commission said on Thursday.
"The Attorney General's Office and the National Institute for Combating Drugs need fundamental reform," the Working Group for Reform of the Attorney General's Office said in a statement.
"The institution in charge of procuring justice has a gigantic structure which is difficult to administer and operate ... Society has lost faith in the institution."
The commission, made up of prominent lawyers, is drawing up recommendations as part of a radical overhaul of the institution announced this week by Attorney General Jorge Madrazo Cuellar.
It said the first priority should be fighting drug-trafficking.
Mexico's top anti-narcotics warrior, army Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, was fired last week and arrested on charges of working for Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the country's most powerful drug baron.
Officials recognise that drugs-related corruption is widespread among Mexico's police forces.

President Bill Clinton must decide by Saturday whether to "certify" that Mexico is cooperating with the United States in its war on drugs. Countries failing the annual U.S. review of anti-narcotics efforts may face U.S. sanctions.

The commission, in its first report, said legal changes would not be enough to stop the rot and that among the requirements for reform were new specialised training programmes for policemen as well as modern computer technology for faster processing of cases.
Earlier on Thursday, the government appointed lawyer Lorenzo Manuel Thomas Torres as Mexico City's new attorney general.

Thomas, 52, took over from Jose Antonio Gonzalez Fernandez, who stepped down on Feb. 7 to run a losing campaign for the candidacy of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) for mayor of Mexico City.
Thomas, who is originally from the northern border city of Tijuana, was until Thursday district director of legal affairs.

Pro-goverment television news programme 24 Horas quoted Enrique Salgado, the capital's secretary of public security, as saying that more than 2,000 army troops would help police Mexico City in the coming days while police agents take specialised training courses.
The report could not immediately be confirmed.
